description: Diganta is a team from BRAC University specialized on small satellite and space system engineering
summary: Landing on the Moon is only half the battle to survive and send back data, a lander needs sunlight for power and an open line of sight to phone home to Earth at the exact same time. We built Ops Window to help space planners, students, and enthusiasts easily see these critical operating windows across 22 real Moon missions, from Apollo 11 all the way to upcoming Artemis polar landings. By turning complex NASA trajectory numbers into interactive 3D sky domes, synchronized maps, and a conversational AI guide, our tool lets anyone explore what it actually takes to keep a spacecraft alive on the lunar surface.
details:
When a spacecraft lands on the Moon, surviving comes down to two simple things happening at the exact same time: having sunlight to charge its solar batteries, and having a clear view of Earth to phone home and send back photos. Because a single day on the Moon lasts about an entire Earth month, two weeks of blazing daylight followed by two weeks of freezing, pitch-black night where temperatures drop to minus 170^∘ "C" . Here timing is everything. If the Sun is up but Earth is hidden behind the Moon, a rover has power but cannot talk to us. If Earth is in view but the Sun has set, it can transmit but quickly runs out of battery and freezes in the dark. Back during the Apollo missions, landing near the equator was relatively easy because Earth hovered permanently high in the sky. But today, the world is heading to the Moon's South Pole to search for frozen water inside deep craters. Down at the pole, the Sun and Earth barely peek above the horizon, meaning even a small crater rim can cast a huge shadow that completely cuts off both power and communication. Before Ops Window, there was no simple tool that let people actually see and compare these make-or-break moments across different Moon landings.

To solve this, we created Ops Window, an interactive web app that runs right in your browser without needing any backend server or installation, and works completely offline once opened. We gathered real flight and landing data from 22 actual lunar missions from Apollo 11 to China's Chang'e missions, India's Chandrayaan-3, Japan's SLIM lander, and the latest commercial lunar landers. Our interactive map streams real satellite photos from NASA, showing where each mission landed and how shadows sweep across the surface. The coolest part is our interactive 3D sky dome, which lets you stand right on the lander's footpad and watch the Sun and Earth trace their paths across the sky. You can switch to a full 360-degree view to see why a far-side mission like Chang'e 4 had Earth hidden deep below its horizon and needed a relay satellite in space, adjust a crater-wall slider to watch shadows physically block out sunlight at polar sites, compare two missions side-by-side, place virtual radio towers on the map to see how a future base could bring signals to blackout zones, and talk with ARTEMIS AI, our built-in mission copilot that explains complex topics like battery life, freezing night temperatures, and radio schedules in everyday, friendly words.

Looking ahead, we want to grow Ops Window from an educational visualizer into a full mission-planning tool for humanity's permanent return to the Moon. First, we plan to plug in NASA's laser elevation maps to calculate real, jagged shadows cast by actual crater walls, boulders, and hills instead of treating the ground as flat. Second, we want to add moving relay satellites in space like the upcoming Lunar Gateway station and China's Queqiao-2, so users can watch orbiting spacecraft pass overhead and see exactly when a stranded rover gets a window to beam its data home. Finally, we want to create a smart route-finder for rovers that automatically maps out paths along sunlit crater rims, helping robot explorers stay in the light and avoid freezing shadow traps. By turning heavy orbital mechanics into something visual, intuitive, and fun to explore, Ops Window helps anyone understand what it really takes to survive on the Moon.
